meta.subtitle: A contracted AI-inference backlog and net cash, priced at a sales multiple in the low sixties after more than halving from its post-IPO high

analystSentiment.commentary:
Cerebras Systems designs wafer-scale processors for AI inference and, since a May 2026 IPO, sells that compute as both hardware and cloud capacity. The market has repriced it hard: the shares are $184.03 against a 52-week range of $160.81 – $386.34, more than a halving from the high, even as the top line compounds, with revenue of $510M in FY25 up 75.7% and $373.5 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026. Behind the quarter sits a remaining performance obligation of $25.4 billion, most of it a December 2025 agreement under which OpenAI committed to 750MW of inference capacity. The Street is almost uniformly positive: 7 Buys, 1 Hold, no Sells, and a consensus target of $300.50, +63.3% above the price.

We rate the shares HOLD, target range $150–$250, well below the Street, because the valuation already prices years of flawless execution. On GAAP the company loses money heavily, the trailing operating margin is deeply negative, and the stock trades at a sales multiple in the low sixties and, on forward earnings, in the triple digits. FY25 net income of $237.8M and diluted EPS of $0.41 look positive only because of gains below the operating line; the FY25 operating margin was -28.5%.

What keeps this from a lower rating is the other side of the ledger. The balance sheet is net cash, liquidity is ample, and the backlog gives revenue visibility few loss-makers have. The probability-weighted fair value of $197.75 sits a touch above the price; the gap to the Street is the discount we take for a business with a limited operating history, disclosed material weaknesses, and revenue concentrated in a handful of customers.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Cerebras Systems, founded in 2015 and based in Sunnyvale, California, builds AI compute around the Wafer-Scale Engine, a processor that occupies an entire silicon wafer; the company describes it as 'the world's first and only commercialized wafer-scale processor' and sells it on inference speed against GPUs. It reaches customers two ways: selling AI systems as hardware for on-premises use, and selling compute as cloud capacity, either dedicated take-or-pay or on-demand. The vendor breaks out no product or geographic revenue split, so we treat the company as the single reportable segment it files as; management's own framing is the split between hardware and cloud-and-services revenue.

The demand base is concentrated in a few large customers. In December 2025 Cerebras signed a master relationship agreement under which OpenAI committed to 750MW of inference capacity, deployed in tranches through 2028, with an option for a further 1.25GW by 2030; that commitment is the bulk of the contracted backlog the growth section quantifies. The risk factors name OpenAI, G42, MBZUAI and AWS as the significant customers, and in June 2026 the company added a hardware-leasing agreement with AWS that had not commenced by quarter-end.

Two structural features shape the equity. Cerebras went public in May 2026, and a multi-class share structure concentrates voting control with pre-IPO holders, executives and directors. The company also discloses material weaknesses in its internal control over financial reporting.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body:
The thesis is that Cerebras is a genuine beneficiary of AI-inference demand, sold at a price that already assumes the backlog converts. The demand is contracted: a large remaining performance obligation, revenue that reached $373.5 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026, and consensus that has it multiplying for years. The balance sheet is net cash, so the company can fund the data-center build-out without the solvency risk that dogs other fast growers.

What holds us at HOLD is the price against the economics. The shares trade at a sales multiple in the low sixties while GAAP losses are heavy and cash is flowing out, and forward earnings multiples stay in the triple digits. Management leans on 'core' figures that strip out non-cash warrant and pass-through effects, but even those show a negative operating margin in the quarter. Our HOLD rests on the backlog and the balance sheet offsetting a valuation that leaves no room for the execution, dilution and concentration risks to bite.

catalysts: RPO conversion: the contracted backlog is the main driver, and the growth section lays out how fast it is scheduled to turn into revenue through 2028.
Margin inflection: management guides its 'core' gross margin toward a 60%-plus target as owned data centers replace rented capacity; the financials section says what would confirm it.
New cloud and hyperscaler deals: AWS availability and other hyperscaler discussions could add backlog beyond the OpenAI base, as the growth section details.
Path to profitability: consensus swings from a loss this year to positive EPS next year, and early evidence of that turn is the catalyst the valuation section is watching.
risks: Valuation: the multiple prices years of execution, so any growth or margin stumble compresses it hard; the valuation section carries the math.
Customer concentration: revenue leans on a few names, OpenAI above all, so a change in that relationship would hit results, as the risk section details.
GAAP losses and dilution: the company funds growth with stock and reports large GAAP losses, and the cash-flow and risk sections carry the size and the dilution.
Governance and controls: disclosed material weaknesses and a multi-class structure that concentrates voting control both sit in the risk section.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The income statement has to be read on two bases, because management reports 'core' figures alongside GAAP and the two diverge sharply. On GAAP, revenue grew from near zero in FY22 to $510M in FY25, a 75.7% gain in the latest year, and the gross margin climbed from 11.7% in FY22 to 39.0% in FY25. Q2'26 GAAP revenue was $180.1 million, up 74% year-over-year. Management's 'core' revenue for the same quarter was $209.9 million, up 103%; the gap reflects the adjustments management makes to reach its 'core' figures, chiefly the non-cash amortization of customer warrants and the pass-through data-center amounts it removes from reported revenue.

Below the gross line the losses are large. The FY25 operating margin was -28.5% and the trailing operating margin is -81.2%, the latter widened by IPO-driven stock compensation. Q2'26 operating margin was -265% on a GAAP basis, against a 'core' operating margin of -16% that management frames as improving from -42% a year earlier. FY25 net income of $237.8M and diluted EPS of $0.41 are positive, but only because of gains below the operating line; operations lost money. The line to watch is whether the core margin keeps climbing toward the company's stated targets as owned capacity replaces rented systems, or whether warrant amortization and pass-through costs keep the reported numbers deeply negative.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.balanceCommentary:
The balance sheet is the strongest part of the story and the reason the downside is a de-rating rather than a solvency event. At FY25 the company held $1.1B of cash and short-term investments against $261.8M of total debt, for net debt of -$439.9M, a net cash position, and the trailing current ratio is 5.82. The IPO in May 2026 added materially to that cash, and the company funds its build-out mainly with equity, alongside a roughly $1.0 billion working capital loan drawn in January 2026 that it repays with non-cash service credits rather than cash.

Two cautions sit alongside the liquidity. Reported total equity was negative through the years shown, -$0.6B at FY25, a feature of the pre-IPO capital structure rather than a sign of insolvency given the net cash position; after the May 2026 IPO that structure looks different. And the growth plan is capital-hungry: the company is building and fitting out data centers, so the cash raised is earmarked for capacity, not a buffer. A reader is paying a rich multiple of sales for a company whose book value is being rebuilt as it scales, and whose share count is rising as it funds itself with stock.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended late December.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash flow is where the investment phase is most visible. Free cash flow was negative $392.8 million in FY25 for a free-cash-flow margin of -77.0%, and capital expenditure was $382.7 million as the company began building owned data-center capacity in earnest. Operating cash flow has been erratic, a $0.5B inflow in FY24 against outflows in the other years shown, so the cash burn reflects the investment programme rather than a failure of operations, but it is real and large relative to the company's revenue base.

The near-term shape is more of the same: the company is buying long-lead capacity and fitting out data centers ahead of the contracted revenue, and it is funding that with the equity it raised at the IPO rather than with cash from operations. Management frames the spend as deliberate, front-loaded investment to capture a backlog that pays out later, and the net-cash balance sheet the balance-sheet section describes is what makes it affordable. Our judgment on cash is that the strategy is coherent and the timing is the risk: the market will not pay a triple-digit forward multiple indefinitely while cash flows out, so the date free cash flow turns matters as much as the growth rate.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
Cerebras cannot be valued on trailing earnings, which are negative, so the debate is what to pay for the growth. The shares trade at 61.2x sales, a P/E of -56.4x on trailing losses and an EV/EBITDA of -72.2x, none of which mean much except that the market is paying for a revenue base it expects to multiply. On forward numbers the picture is only a little less extreme: consensus revenue is $885.3M for FY26 and $2.9B for FY27, and on FY27E EPS of $1.24 the multiple is about 148.4x. The company pays no dividend.

The Street is close to unanimous and far above the price: 8 analysts, 7 Buys, 1 Hold and no Sells, a consensus target of $300.50, a median of $300.00 and a range of $279.00–$330.00 whose low end still sits well above today's $184.03. Our view is more cautious. The growth and the backlog are real, but a multiple this high on a company with GAAP losses, negative free cash flow and a limited operating history warrants a target below the Street and a wide range, because the same multiple that lifts the shares if execution holds is what compresses them if it slips.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The AI-inference build-out plays out: the contracted backlog converts on schedule, cloud capacity ramps as OpenAI and later hyperscalers deploy, core margins climb toward the company's 60%-plus target, and the market re-rates the shares back toward the Street's consensus as losses narrow.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue compounds roughly in line with consensus, but heavy GAAP losses, ongoing dilution and customer concentration keep the multiple from expanding, so the shares hold near today's level after their fall from the high.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: AI-infrastructure spending cools or the OpenAI relationship changes, warrant amortization and pass-through costs keep reported results deeply negative, the material weaknesses or a dilutive capital raise unsettle holders, and a multiple built on future earnings compresses hard.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base case at 45%, the Bull at 30% and the Bear at 25%, for a probability-weighted fair value of $197.75, a high-single-digit percentage above the price and inside the HOLD envelope; the $150–$250 target range brackets the Base. The Base case is growth delivered without a re-rating, which from a price that has already fallen from the high leaves the shares roughly where they are. The Bull case is the backlog converting into scale and margin and a re-rating toward the Street; we give it three chances in ten because the demand is contracted but the reported economics are years from catching up. The Bear case carries a full quarter of the weight because a rich sales multiple gives the shares a long way to fall, and the risks that would trigger it, concentration, dilution and control weaknesses, are concrete.

A move to BUY would need the core margin to keep inflecting and free cash flow to turn toward positive on schedule, with the backlog visibly converting into reported revenue. A move to SELL would follow a cut to the growth outlook, a control failure that proves costly, or an AI-spending pullback that strands the capacity being built.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Cerebras files as a single reportable segment, so the moat reads at the level of the whole company. Revenue comes two ways that management describes but the vendor data does not split: hardware, the sale of AI systems for on-premises use; and cloud and other services, the dedicated take-or-pay and on-demand capacity that management expects to become the larger share as the OpenAI deployment ramps. The engine of the business is the Wafer-Scale Engine and the inference speed it is built to deliver. The durability question is whether that speed advantage, and the switching costs once a customer builds its stack around it, hold up against far larger competitors. And because revenue is concentrated in a few customers, OpenAI above all, the segment's fortunes track a handful of relationships rather than a diversified book.

moatFactors.name: Wafer-scale performance
moatFactors.body: Cerebras's edge is the Wafer-Scale Engine, which the company describes as 'the world's first and only commercialized wafer-scale processor' and positions on inference speed against GPU-based systems. Speed is a real differentiator in inference, where latency shapes user engagement and cost per token. The counter is that performance leadership in silicon is defended only by continuous reinvestment, against far larger competitors in GPUs with vastly bigger research budgets, and a single design win lost or leapfrogged can erode the advantage quickly.

moatFactors.name: Contracted backlog
moatFactors.body: The remaining performance obligation, most of it the OpenAI capacity commitment, gives Cerebras revenue visibility that few loss-making companies have, and it funds the confidence to build capacity ahead of demand. The counter is that the backlog is concentrated in one customer and depends on that customer's deployment schedule and continued funding; the company's own risk factors flag that a change in the OpenAI relationship would harm results, so the backlog is a moat only as far as it actually converts.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs in inference
moatFactors.body: Management argues that once customers adopt fast inference, expectations for interactivity rise and engineering teams move on, making it hard to return to slower systems. There is logic to that lock-in, and take-or-pay cloud contracts reinforce it. The counter is that the company has a limited operating history at this scale, the inference-cloud market is nascent, and customers reaching Cerebras through partner marketplaces retain alternatives; the switching cost is asserted more than proven.

moatFactors.name: Supply and manufacturing access
moatFactors.body: Cerebras depends on TSMC for wafers and on contract manufacturers such as Flex and Sanmina to build systems, and management frames its supplier relationships and wafer access as an advantage in a supply-constrained market. The counter, which the risk factors state plainly, is that substantially all manufacturing and components are procured on purchase orders without capacity or volume commitments, and several inputs are sole-sourced, so the supply chain is a dependency as much as an edge.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow: real enough to protect the revenue already under contract, not wide enough to justify the multiple the market is paying. What lasts is the technology lead in inference speed, the switching costs once a customer builds around it, and a backlog that funds the next stage of growth. What does not last on its own is pricing power against far larger rivals, or a customer base concentrated in a few names in a market that is still forming. The widening path is diversification, more hyperscaler and enterprise customers, recurring cloud revenue, and margins that thicken as owned capacity replaces rented systems. The narrowing path is an AI-spending slowdown, a stumble against better-funded competitors, or a change in the OpenAI relationship. We rate the moat narrow because the technology and the backlog clearly protect what Cerebras has, and do not clearly earn the returns the valuation assumes.

points: The backlog is the growth: management points to a remaining performance obligation of $25.4 billion, most of it OpenAI's committed inference capacity deployed through 2028, and says it expects to more than triple its core revenue in 2027. The counter is that the risk factors warn against relying on past growth rates and the deployment schedule is the customer's to set.

Cloud is becoming the larger business: management expects cloud and other services to grow as a share of revenue as the OpenAI deployment ramps, and reported core cloud and other services revenue of $127.7 million in the quarter, up 287% year-over-year. The mix shift matters because cloud is where the take-or-pay contracts and the margin-expansion story sit.

Capacity is the constraint and the plan: management says it has more than 600 megawatts of data-center capacity live or under contract for delivery by the end of 2027, with a pipeline measured in gigawatts, and is scaling manufacturing with its partners. The counter is that building and filling that capacity is capital-intensive and is what drives the cash outflow.

New customers and markets add optionality: beyond OpenAI, management cited an AWS agreement and named customers in coding and agentic software, though hyperscaler revenue is not expected until mid-2027 and is not yet in the backlog.

management.leadership: Cerebras is led by the founding management team that built it from 2015 and took it public in May 2026. On the earnings call, management frames 2026 as a foundation-building year for multiples of growth in 2027 and beyond, and the strategy is consistent: win large capacity commitments, build data-center and manufacturing capacity ahead of demand, and push the technology roadmap on inference speed. The record that supports the strategy is the revenue ramp and the contracted backlog; the reservation is that the team is asking the market to fund a deeply loss-making, capital-hungry build-out on the promise that reported economics catch up later, and that it does so having disclosed material weaknesses in financial controls. The pack carries no proxy statement, so we make no claim on board composition or the specifics of executive pay beyond the IPO-linked stock compensation the filing describes.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is single-minded and equity-funded: internally funded investment in data-center capacity, manufacturing and R&D, at the capital-expenditure and free-cash-flow levels the cash-flow section sizes, ahead of the revenue that is contracted to come. The company raised fresh equity in its May 2026 IPO to fund most of the build-out, and the borrowing it does carry, including the working capital loan tied to the OpenAI arrangement, is repaid largely in service credits rather than cash. There are no dividends and no buybacks of consequence, which is right for a company at this stage. The funding choice keeps the balance sheet net cash, as the balance-sheet section describes, but it dilutes: the share count is rising as the company issues stock, including a large IPO-linked grant to its CTO, so per-share value depends on the investments earning more than the new shares cost. Our judgment is that the allocation is coherent with the opportunity and that its discipline will be tested by whether the capacity converts to profitable revenue before the market tires of the cash outflow and the dilution.
management.governance: The pack carries no proxy statement, so the usual governance detail, board composition and independence, the audit committee, executive pay tables and related-party policy, is not available to quote, and we make no claim on it. Two governance features do appear in the 10-Q itself and matter to holders. First, a multi-class share structure concentrates voting control with pre-IPO stockholders, including executives, employees and directors and their affiliates, which limits the influence of public Class A holders over corporate matters. Second, the company has disclosed material weaknesses in its internal control over financial reporting; until they are remediated, there is a higher risk that the statements contain errors, which is a real concern for a company whose GAAP and 'core' figures already diverge sharply. Governance here is not a control structure a public holder can lean on, and the reporting-control gap raises the bar for trusting the numbers.

idiosyncratic: Valuation risk dominates. On the sales and forward-earnings multiples the valuation section sets out, the shares price years of execution, so a growth or margin disappointment compresses the multiple from a great height; the fall from a 52-week high of $386.34 to $184.03 over recent months shows how far that can go. The net-cash balance sheet means the downside is a de-rating rather than an impairment, but a de-rating from this height is severe.

Customer concentration. A substantial portion of revenue comes from a few customers, and the risk factors name OpenAI, G42, MBZUAI and AWS; OpenAI alone underpins most of the backlog. A reduction in demand from, or a deterioration in the relationship with, any of them, OpenAI above all, would hit revenue and the backlog at once.

GAAP losses, cash burn and dilution. The company reports large GAAP losses and negative free cash flow, which the cash-flow section sizes, and it funds itself by issuing stock, so holders face both continued losses and dilution until the model turns. The market's patience for a loss-maker at this multiple is finite.

Reporting-control and structural risks. The company has disclosed material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting, and a multi-class structure concentrates voting control with insiders. Both raise the risk premium: one because the numbers themselves carry more uncertainty, the other because public holders have little say if management's choices disappoint.

Legal overhang. In late June and early July 2026, multiple law firms announced securities-fraud investigations into the company, as the headlines show; such investigations often follow a volatile new listing, but they add cost and distraction and signal litigation risk.
risks.systemic: The systemic exposure is the AI-infrastructure spending cycle. Cerebras's demand rests on hyperscalers, foundation-model labs and sovereign-AI buyers continuing to commit capital to inference compute; the same wave that created the backlog could ebb if AI monetization disappoints or the capital cycle turns, and a company building capacity years ahead of revenue is exposed to that timing. Concentrated demand makes it sharper: much of the industry's inference spend flows through a few large buyers, so a pause by one of them moves the whole market. Layered on top are supply-chain dependence on TSMC and a handful of contract manufacturers, and U.S. export controls that limit where advanced AI systems can be sold. The offset is that the secular shift toward AI inference is real and, if it holds, supports demand across the cycle; the systemic risk is one of timing, concentration and policy more than of the end-market disappearing.

body: **HOLD, target range $150–$250.** Cerebras sits in the middle of the AI-inference build-out with a contracted backlog, a net-cash balance sheet and a technology lead in inference speed, and the shares have already fallen from their post-IPO high. But the valuation still asks for near-flawless execution, and a probability-weighted fair value of $197.75 sits only a little above the price. That balance, real and funded demand against a price that already reflects it, is what earns the HOLD rather than a buy.

We stop well short of the Street because the risks are concrete, not hypothetical. The company loses money on a GAAP basis, funds itself with dilutive equity, and carries the concentration, control and structural risks the risk section details, all while trading on multiples of sales and forward earnings that leave no room for a stumble. The growth we believe; the price already pays for it, and then some.

The conditions that would move us up to BUY or down to SELL are set out in the valuation section; in short, the rating rises if the reported economics start catching up to the backlog, and falls if the growth, the controls or the AI-spending cycle crack.
